where: On the calibration grid (Figure 1) Wu-Manber is fastest in 116 of the 240 cases: it owns almost every cell with many patterns and m ≥ 12, because its shift grows with the shortest pattern length and it is nearly insensitive to the number of patterns. Aho-Corasick wins with many (k ≥ 16) very short (m = 4) patterns, where Wu-Manber's shift drops to 1–2 characters. With a single pattern (k = 1) the winner depends on the alphabet and on m: for long patterns (m ≥ 48) the q-gram based bm4DNAHMbs takes 12 of 24 cases; for short and medium patterns bm4DNADS, Boyer-Moore and Horspool are neck and neck. Shift-Or takes 7 of its 8 wins at m = 4. At n = 10³ preprocessing dominates, and Rabin-Karp, which has the smallest table, wins 26 of 60 cases. Suffix array, FM-index and KMP never win on the grid: building an index costs more than a single-pass search, and KMP never skips. The two atoms of Allmer's rule (DS, HMbs) are together fastest in only 21% of the grid, which explains why the rule is 2.3× slower when there are many patterns.
wrong: Nearly equal estimates. Most wrong choices are cases where the top two estimates are within 5–15% of each other. In V87 (binary alphabet, k = 5) the top four estimates lie between 0.379 and 0.426 ms; the chosen Rabin-Karp took 0.58 ms in one measurement and 1.20 ms in the next on the same case. This shows that below 1 ms, measurement noise is of the same size as the model's error. In R7 (E. coli stream, a single pattern of length 150) the estimates for Horspool and bm4DNADS differ by 2.5%.

Alphabet not seen in calibration. V63 and V117 (binary alphabet, k ≈ 90, long patterns) are examples of the most frequent wrong pair, "Wu-Manber instead of Aho-Corasick". With σ = 2 almost every B-gram is in the shift table, so Wu-Manber's real average shift is shorter than the model predicts. The model never saw a binary alphabet and generalises only through Σf². Even so, the slowdown in these two cases stays at 1.9×.

Very short times. In S26 and V76 the fastest atom finishes in 40 µs. The estimates are around 0.14 ms and the constant "base" term dominates. As the assignment's FAQ also suggests, we do not interpret differences below 0.1 ms; these cases are large in ratio but negligible in absolute time.

An error fixed with the stream prior. The first version of the model looked at the first record of the 126-record E. coli stream (n = 207) and chose the suffix array. This was the right choice for that single record (0.26 ms against 0.29 ms), but because the index is rebuilt for every record, the whole stream became 16× slower. We split the cost into "per run" (pattern preprocessing) and "per record" (scanning, indexing) parts and treat a short first record as part of a stream of ≈ 2¹⁶ characters. With this change the worst slowdown on the real data set dropped from 16.0× to 3.3×. The change did not touch the measurement data; it only changed the structure of the model, and validation was run again.
limits: The decision looks only at the first record (as the contract requires). In a stream whose first record is very different from the rest, the decision can be poor. The stream prior (at most 128 records, ≈ 2¹⁶ characters) is an assumption and can be changed with the expectedRecords parameter.

End-to-end overhead. The decision (shape + 11 estimates + building the atom) takes about 0.2 ms (median). Because the fastest atom takes less than 0.2 ms in 32% of the validation cases, the geometric mean measured including the decision rises to 1.69. On the 44 cases where the fastest time is ≥ 1 ms this value is 1.18. On long inputs the cost of the decision is negligible.

Calibration on one machine. The coefficients were measured on an Intel Xeon with Node 22. A different JIT or cache structure can change the ranking; the "measure all atoms" button on the site shows this in the browser. Recalibration is a single command (npm run calibrate, ~4 min).

The model is simple. Each atom has at most 6 linear terms; cache effects, branch prediction and the cost of output sorting that grows with k are modelled only approximately. The in-sample median relative error ranges from 8% (Horspool) to 24% (FM-index) (Appendix B).
Estimating σ. For first records longer than 8,192 characters the frequencies come from a sample; a very rare character may be missed. This does not affect correctness, only the estimate.
Memory. Aho-Corasick keeps a full DFA (states × S), and FM-index keeps the full SA. For very large pattern sets or texts, memory becomes the limit before speed does.
